title: Building a Supercharged Lexus GS 430: First Drive - thetruthaboutcars.com
content: We wrap up a few small but important details on our supercharged 2001 Lexus GS430 before uploading a custom All4Swap tune to the factory ECU so we can experience for the first time what this Range Rover TVS1900 supercharger can really do on the stock 3UZ V8 engine. Speed Academy is a website and YouTube channel based on making things go fast and enjoying cars. Peter Tarach and Dave Pratte are the forces behind Speed Academy. The TTAC Creators Series tells stories and amplifies creators from all corners of the car world, including culture, dealerships, collections, modified builds and more. An AI-produced summary of the transcript, edited by a staffer, is below. Become a TTAC insider. Get the latest news, features, TTAC takes, and everything else that gets to the truth about cars first by  subscribing to our newsletter. The transcript follows the final stages of a $6,000 2001 Lexus GS 430 build, which began life as a clean luxury sedan but has been transformed into a supercharged sleeper with a budget Range Rover supercharger, TRD-style body kit, upgraded suspension, custom headlights and other performance and cosmetic modifications. The goal is to resolve the remaining bugs, load a custom ECU tune and finally see how the car performs. The first job is refinishing the supercharger intake tube. The large logo and chrome finish are replaced with a wrinkle-black VHT coating, giving the engine bay a cleaner, more understated appearance. The paint turns out well despite a small dent and scratch caused by dropping the tube. The team also addresses a check-engine light caused by the EVAP system. Because the modified intake/supercharger setup left an EVAP sensor improperly plumbed, they connect it to a vacuum source between the throttle body and supercharger. They also fix the intercooler heat-exchanger pump, which was receiving constant power from the fuse box even with the ignition off. The solution is to connect it to switched power from the headlight wiring. The GS 430 has custom projector headlights using Q45-style projector lenses, but the existing setup wasn't producing enough light. The car actually had factory wiring for HID headlights, so the team installs an HID system. One bulb turns out to be broken and requires replacement, but once installed, the HIDs produce substantially better illumination. The custom headlights also receive a ceramic sealant to protect their appearance. A major step is loading the All for Swaps custom tune supplied by Brandon at Quantum Auto. Rather than simply sending the ECU away for a one-time flash, the team invests in the necessary PCM Flash cable, dongle and software so the ECU can be modified again in the future if the car receives larger injectors or a higher-boost pulley. Both the TCU and ECU maps are flashed, giving the GS 430 its first opportunity to run at full power. The driver's door has several problems, including an inoperative power mirror and a key-fob locking issue. Inspection reveals no obvious broken wires in the door harness. Cleaning the mirror-switch contacts unexpectedly restores its operation, although the switch itself appears worn and only works reliably when pushed aggressively. The key-fob problem proves more difficult. The wiring is poorly soldered, so it is cleaned up, but that doesn't solve the issue. The team successfully puts the car into key-fob programming mode and establishes communication between the fob and car, yet the locks still don't respond. After roughly 20 attempts at reprogramming, the problem remains unresolved, possibly pointing to a module or another electrical fault. The aftermarket TRD gauge cluster looks impressive, with a 320-km/h speedometer and 9,000-rpm tachometer, but it is badly calibrated for the GS 430's engine. At an actual 100 km/h, for example, it reads approximately 120 km/h. Because the cluster was originally designed for an Aristo and its calibration doesn't match the GS 430's UZ-series engine, there is no simple fix. The team therefore removes it and reinstalls the stock gauge cluster, sacrificing some visual flair for accurate readings. With the ECU/TCU tune installed and the remaining major mechanical work completed, the GS 430 finally gets its first full-power test drive. The supercharged V8 delivers a noticeable increase in performance, with the larger supercharger providing stronger acceleration than the builder's previous LS 430 equipped with a smaller M12 blower. Power delivery is described as smooth, with crisp transmission shifts, although the transmission itself feels somewhat dated. The supercharger whine is audible without overwhelming the exhaust note, giving the car the desired sleeper character. The reviewers are particularly impressed with how quick the GS 430 feels after the tune. The car's Tein Flex Z coilovers with EDFC5 electronic damping control also receive a positive review. The system automatically adjusts damping based on road conditions and information from its accelerometers/G-force sensors and GPS. Despite costing roughly $1,000 for the coilovers and another $700–$800 for the EDFC system, the setup provides a surprisingly comfortable and sophisticated ride. The GS 430 is substantially less floaty than before, yet it remains smooth and planted. It handles normal bumps exceptionally well, although it can crash over particularly severe bumps at high speed. The combination of the suspension and Continental tires significantly improves the car's handling and reduces the body roll that previously made the GS 430 feel like a boat. The project is considered a major success. The supercharged GS 430 combines sleeper looks, substantial power, improved handling and a surprisingly comfortable ride, all while maintaining the character of an old luxury sedan. The builder is especially pleased with the supercharger's sound and performance and considers the car essentially finished. However, the actual horsepower figures have not yet been revealed. A final episode will put the car on a dyno and compare it in a roll race against Pete's BMW M5. Bottom line: What started as a $6,000 2001 Lexus GS 430 has evolved into a genuinely quick, extensively modified sleeper. The build still has a few unresolved electrical quirks, but the important parts — the supercharged powertrain, tune, suspension and overall driving experience — have exceeded expectations. Speed Academy is a website and YouTube channel based on making things go fast and enjoying cars. Peter Tarach and Dave Pratte are the forces behind Speed Academy. title: JPM, GS, MS Stocks Edge Higher After-Hours — Banks Lift Dividends And Announce Buybacks After Fed Stress Test - Stocktwits
content: Shares of JPMorgan Chase & Co (JPM), Morgan Stanley (MS) and Goldman Sachs (GS) edged higher in after-hours trading on Wednesday after the banks announced higher dividends and buybacks following the Federal Reserve’s stress test, which showed the banking sector remains well positioned to withstand a severe economic downturn. At the time of writing, JPM stock was up 0.6% after-hours after closing the regular session down 0.21%, while MS shares gained 0.4% and GS stock was up 0.1%. JPMorgan Chase & Co announced a $50-billion share repurchase program and raised its quarterly dividend as part of updated shareholder return plans. The bank said its board also intends to increase its quarterly dividend 10% to $1.65 per share, up from $1.50 per share, for the third quarter of 2026. The new buyback program will take effect from July 1, alongside the updated shareholder return plans. Jamie Dimon, Chairman and CEO of JPMorgan Chase, said, “The Board’s intended dividend increase is supported by our consistent investment in our business and strong financial performance. The new share repurchase program provides us with the flexibility to deploy capital in ways that enhance shareholder value over time.” Goldman Sachs (GS) also increased its quarterly dividend by 11% to $5 per share from $4.50, pointing to strong earnings momentum and a robust capital position. The revised payout implies an annual dividend of $20 and will take effect on July 1, pending board approval. Morgan Stanley (MS) similarly announced a 15% hike in its quarterly dividend to $1.15 per share from $1. In addition, the firm said its board has reauthorized a multi-year share repurchase program of up to $20 billion, with no fixed end date, set to begin in the third quarter. The announcement by JPMorgan Chase & Co comes after the U.S. Federal Reserve released the results of its annual stress test. It showed that large banks are well positioned to withstand a severe recession and continue lending to households and businesses. The Fed said that despite more than $708 billion in total loan losses under the hypothetical scenario, aggregate capital declined only 1.6 percentage points and remained above minimum requirements. It added that all 32 banks tested stayed above their minimum common equity tier 1 capital requirements under a scenario that included a severe global recession, a 39% drop in commercial real estate prices, a 30% fall in house prices and an unemployment rate peaking at 10%. SpaceX shares rose 1% premarket on Wednesday, bucking concerns over rising short interest, lockup-related selling pressure, and a former SEC chair’s warning that IPO excitement could give way to a “great rebalancing.” SPCX stock fell as low as $147.11 early Tuesday, slipping below the $150 level from its first Nasdaq trading day after the June 11 IPO. The stock later recovered, ending Tuesday up about 1% at near $156. About 40 million SpaceX shares are currently sold short, representing roughly 5% to 7% of the company’s publicly tradable float of about 625 million shares, according to S3 Partners. Borrow conditions also do not point to the squeeze pressure. More than 30 million SpaceX shares are available to borrow, while annualized borrowing fees are below 1%, S3 said, according to CNBC. “SPCX has attracted active short-selling interest, but the data suggest this is far from a supply-constrained short,” said Matthew Unterman, head of research at S3. “The current setup looks more like normal price discovery than a classic short-squeeze candidate.” Coatue investor said in a CNBC interview that the firm is not rushing to cash out. When asked whether Coatue would keep or sell its SpaceX shares, he said, “I’m going to keep them,” noting that the shares must be held for six months after receipt. After the lockup, he said the decision becomes “more of a portfolio decision,” based on how large SpaceX becomes relative to the rest of the firm’s holdings. “We own a significant amount of SpaceX,” he said, while adding that some of his biggest mistakes came from “optimizing for the short run.” He pointed to Nvidia as a lesson, calling his decision to sell “one of the bigger mistakes” he had made. “Sometimes you’re like, ‘Oh, maybe I’m so clever. I can sell out of this and buy that.’ It rarely works,” he said. Former SEC Chair Gary Gensler offered a more cautious view, saying that the wave of mega IPOs, including SpaceX, could be a “tell” about where the market cycle stands. He said that markets are funding a major AI infrastructure boom, but warned that some valuations are running at “100, 140 times revenues without earnings,” according to Bloomberg. Gensler said it is possible that the market looks back in six months and finds the IPO wave was “fine.” However, he also warned there is an “equal and better chance” that venture capitalists and sovereign wealth funds begin selling as lockups expire. “I call it the great rebalancing,” Gensler said. “All those venture capitalists and sovereign wealth funds, they’re going to want to take risk off the page.” He said tha investors could move to reduce “a third, a half, maybe three quarters” of their exposure, creating “a lot of selling pressure” as shares become available. title: Mailbag: Reviewing Vikings Week vs. Ravens; Young Defensive Linemen Noticed by Fans - Minnesota Vikings
content: Do you have a comment or question? Send it to the Mailbag. Every Monday we'll post several comments and/or questions. Click here to submit a comment or question to Mailbag. Remember to include your name and town in the email. If Twitter / X is your jam, you can send a question to me that way as well. The Vikings hosted their lone home preseason game Saturday and fell 13-3 to the Ravens, but the big-picture item of the week was the feeling of having accomplished several items and identifying others to work on during the two joint practices between Minnesota and Baltimore. In my years of covering joint practices, I'd say the defenses for both teams usually win the first day, which is not dissimilar from the first day of padded training camp practices each year (that happened again this year at Vikings camp). Such was the case Wednesday, except for the 2-minute drill in which Kyler Murray and J.J. McCarthy each led touchdown drives. Minnesota's offense evened things out a bit more on Thursday while its defense remained dominant. Even though it was truly great to return to U.S. Bank Stadium Saturday for the first time since Week 18 on Jan. 4, the game action felt a little bit anticlimactic because of a couple ups and downs for McCarthy, who got the start with the second-team offense. McCarthy did a great job of feeling pressure, climbing the pocket and giving Tai Felton a great opportunity on a 50-50 ball that went for 50. But the QB with 10 career regular-season starts under his belt lamented execution in the red zone on a second-and-goal pass from the 3 and a fourth-and-goal from the 1. On the other side of the ball, rookies Caleb Banks and Domonique Orange relished their first opportunity at U.S. Bank Stadium, as well as another opportunity to advance their development with meaningful snaps. Minnesota will close its preseason by visiting Denver at 8 p.m. (CT) Friday. Before we get to some questions, I'd like to say it was such a treat to welcome Hub Meeds and his family to the Minnesota Vikings Museum on Thursday. Meeds visited dressed in regalia befitting what he wore on the sidelines as the team's live mascot for more than two decades (1970-92). Meeds' iconic look originated at Super Bowl IV when he and his brother-in-law, Dan Jeans, rented costumes before heading to New Orleans. Meeds, a White Bear Lake truck driver, and Jeans, a St. Paul hair stylist, had tickets to the game, but approached a player gate at Tulane Stadium. Officials mistakenly let them onto the field. Meeds, who had played football at Stillwater High School, liked the view from the sidelines and asked the Vikings if he could become the team's mascot. He was with the team in an official capacity at their next three Super Bowls. Meeds worked home games until 1992 and attended the final game at the Metrodome. After first using a fake beard, Meeds grew the real deal. He also found a 36-inch sword that was made in Germany in 1888 and fashioned a shield. The sword and shield are on display at the Museum in an area that pays tribute to Metropolitan Stadium. Meeds' iconic look was even featured as the cover of the team's 1973 media guide, which happens to be one of the ones mounted on the pillar of Vikings.com's assigned area in the press box. Viktor the Viking, who launched in 2007, was excited to meet Meeds at the Minnesota Vikings Museum. Both enjoyed posing for pictures with guests, and it was wonderful to see multiple generations of Vikings fans connecting at the exhibits. Vikings fans have shown their enthusiasm and devotion to the team in a variety of ways, including the way they dress for home and away games, further linking themselves to their team. Lastly, I'll note that everyone should be on the lookout tomorrow for the unveiling of the Vikings Rivalries uniforms, which will be worn by the team for the first time on Dec. 20 when Minnesota hosts the Detroit Lions. View game action photos from the Vikings preseason game vs. the Ravens at U.S. Bank Stadium. Two preseason games in the books. For the second consecutive week, the second unit offensive line was bad. Nothing to write home about. Ground game couldn't get going, six pressures allowed on 11 dropbacks for McCarthy, and another crippling penalty that wiped out a first down. When opportunity was there, McCarthy continued to miss. Four open receivers he couldn't hit. Still throwing too hard and too high. The defense on the other hand looked very good. Tyler Huntley is a very experienced and quality backup QB. He looked awful and very uncomfortable. The D-line looks to have very strong depth. Banks and "Big Citrus" both looked much more settled into NFL football. One game left to get it together. What are the dates for roster cuts? Do they have to cut to 53 in one shot, or is it still broken up through camp? — Roman B., counting down the days until kickoff against Green Bay from Grand Forks, North Dakota In a couple of aspects, Saturday's game reminded me a bit of last year's regular-season game against the Ravens. The reasons were beyond the plentiful purple and centered on McCarthy's day. Both games featured a completion of 50-plus yards by McCarthy, as well as some misses on passes he wishes were completed. Both games also included some leaks along the offensive line. In the regular season last November, the Ravens racked up 12 QB hits on McCarthy. On Saturday, the group hit him four times across Minnesota's final two possessions of the first quarter, including a couple at the knee or below (no flags were thrown on either). One of those hits occurred when he stayed in the pocket and uncorked a beautiful pass to Jeshaun Jones for a gain of 19 on a third-and-13, but the positive was erased because of a holding penalty against Henry Byrd, who has worked at tackle this season after spending earlier seasons on the interior. No one on social media is pointing out that execution by McCarthy. With the Vikings resting starting tackles Christian Darrisaw and Brian O'Neill, and rookie Caleb Tiernan working his way back from an ankle injury in the preseason opener, the Vikings opted to start veteran Ryan Van Demark at right tackle and Byrd at left tackle. Both defenses stymied the ground game. There was only one run the entire game for 10 or more yards (a 15-yarder for Jermar Jefferson who finished with two carries for 15 yards), so that didn't help any quarterback who played. I'm in the camp that McCarthy has improved certain aspects of his game this offseason, but the Vikings didn't establish the running game the way they did early at New York, and the protection didn't hold for McCarthy on some passes. The play that has generated the most alacrity on social media is the missed throw on fourth-and-goal from the 1. There's a bit of nuance that has been left out. The outside linebacker for the Ravens, Ethan Burke, is 6-foot-6 with 33-inch arms and synched his jump to maximize its effect thanks to a little hitch at the top of the drop by McCarthy. That pressure caused a high throw out of reach of Price. I'm not going to pretend to be a coach, but perhaps a quicker release (before the defender can get his arms up or a pump fake and then release after the OLB lands might have helped a better outcome. I'm also quite bullish on the long-term combination of Banks and Orange, especially in the context of a really encouraging group of players that also includes Jalen Redmond and Levi Drake Rodriguez, a pair of absolute hosses. Banks and Orange were drafted where they were because of some pretty incredible traits that are fun for Defensive Coordinator Brian Flores to add to his concoction. The deadline for teams to reduce their rosters from 90 to 53 is 5 p.m. (CT) on Sunday, Aug. 30, but reductions could happen at any point between Friday's preseason finale and that deadline. Teams could make claims on players subject to the waiver process, so there could be some more fluidity. Practice squads of up to 17 (if one is an International Player) can then be formed next Monday. I have to admit I felt a little sick to my stomach with Minnesota's effort against Baltimore, but then I felt better after I saw that a bunch of starters didn't suit up. So it was second and third stringers trying to make an impression ahead of cutdown days. Although I wondered if it was fourth and fifth stringers manning the o-line. They do realize they're not playing Pop Warner, right? There's no participation trophies in the NFL. Even so, did the QBs have to act like a pillar of strength, or a mannequin? Isn't that why they have legs? But I'm guessing the Vikings may not be able to keep four quarterbacks on the 53-man roster, so the odd man out will have to hope they get signed to the practice squad or another team. But I'm pretty sure the team invested too much in J.J., so I doubt they'll release him. Which means Wentz or Brosmer will draw the short straw. But with roster cuts coming up, I don't know what the numbers are and when they fall, but there's just one preseason game left, so who looks like they've put in the extra effort to survive the first or second cuts? And has Hitman Harry officially hung up his cleats, or is his protracted indecision causing anxiety for rookies in the secondary? After the game and watching the highlights I do feel a bit queasy. And September is just around the corner, so for those who want to be wearing Purple come December, or eternally hopeful for late January and February, they need some urgency and some "dawg" in their play style. — David A. (from the North Shore but melting in the South) I mentioned Minnesota's thinness of experienced players at tackle in the above answer. In addition to sacking McCarthy once, the Ravens dropped Carson Wentz and Max Brosmer twice each and totaled nine QB hits. That's less than ideal when trying to give McCarthy and Brosmer developmental reps. It's accurate to categorize Wentz as a known commodity, given his 99 career regular-season starts that included five with Minnesota in 2025. Head Coach Kevin O'Connell was disappointed with nine penalties, including six on offense that seemed to undermine the establishment of rhythm in Saturday's game. The Vikings have had their depth at safety tested, with Jakobe Thomas experiencing back tightness for multiple weeks and with Theo Jackson leaving during the joint practices during a deep play. It looked like Jamal Adams was going to help out there and potentially at inside linebacker before his heartbreaking, season-ending injury at New York. Undrafted rookie Jacob Thomas has capitalized on the extra reps. I wanted to share an idea about how I believe the Vikings could use the preseason to create an advantage heading into the regular season. My suggestion is to treat the three preseason games as three additional opportunities to prepare our starting team before the games actually count. The NFL gives every team three games with no consequences to their regular-season record. I believe we should take full advantage of that. Rather than using preseason games primarily to determine the depth chart, I would use training camp practices for that purpose. Let players compete every day for their positions and establish who has earned the right to play. Then, when the preseason games begin, play our starters. What the opposing team chooses to do with its own lineup shouldn't really matter. Whether they play their starters, backups or third-string players, our objective should be preparing the Vikings. The value isn't necessarily who is lined up across from us. The value is getting our starting players into an actual NFL game environment. They get to experience the speed of the game, communication, timing, substitutions, play-calling, situational football and the process of playing together under game conditions. If we're destroying the other team, take the starters out. If we're up by a significant margin after three quarters, there is little reason to keep exposing them. Let the backups finish the game. But if we're not playing well, or the game is competitive, keep the starters on the field and use the opportunity. If everything is going well, you've gotten your starters meaningful reps and can get them out early. If things aren't going well, you have another quarter — and potentially another preseason game — to work on it before anything counts. You're essentially being given three games to identify and correct problems for free. I also believe this approach would make roster evaluation more effective. Instead of relying heavily on third-string players playing against third-string players, use training camp to evaluate those players against the Vikings' best players every day. A young offensive lineman shouldn't need four quarters against another team's third-string defensive line to determine whether he belongs. Coaches can learn a tremendous amount by watching him compete against the Vikings' starting defensive line throughout training camp. Then the preseason games can serve their most important purpose: Preparing the players who are actually expected to carry the team during the regular season. The Vikings have three games where a loss doesn't hurt the standings. I believe that's an opportunity that shouldn't be wasted. If we're dominating, pull the starters. If we're not, keep working. Either way, we're using those three games to make the team better before Week 1. Thank you for taking the time to consider my perspective. O'Connell prioritizes the joint practices as two of the best days of training camp to prepare first and second teamers for the regular season. The benefits include the number of snaps that can be accomplished each day, as well as going through some scripted and unscripted scenarios in a controlled environment that hopefully makes teams less susceptible to injuries. That means a preseason game at the end of a week of joint practices is likely to have third stringers or folks further down the depth chart in for most of the time, and the players who are suited up won't have gone through as many preparation reps, which are still few, during the week. Five years ago, Irv Smith, Jr., was entering his third pro season, and the Vikings had designed some plays to create mismatches for him. On the heels of catching 30 passes for 365 yards and five touchdowns in 2020, Smith was looking good in camp. For some reason, Smith was playing in the third preseason contest at Kansas City and suffered a season-ending injury. Fellow tight end Tyler Conklin went on to have a breakout season with 61 catches for 593 yards and three touchdowns, but I have wondered what the combo of Smith and Conklin could have done in 12 personnel and how that duplicity may have helped other aspects of the offense. O'Connell also believes in the importance of developing younger players. To that end, the preseason contests offer in-game reps, even though the scoreboard results don't matter. In a league where every regular-season game means so much, it's weird to think a team can have different goals not necessarily tied to the final score in the preseason, but that's likely going to be the case. Our defense is going to be our strength. Banks and Orange were very disruptive and will make for an awesome rotation. It is too early to throw J.J. out or even drop him to third-string. Who did J.J. play against? Who did Carson play against? Both of them will help us in my opinion. We have a good QB room. How did Walter Rouse play? He moved inside and did a great pancake block on that poor Baltimore DB. Every game in the NFC North will be tough. Skol to this season, Minnesota's defense is showing signs of being extremely difficult to deal with. On back-to-back days, the first team seemed to cause headaches throughout the Baltimore offense led by two-time NFL MVP Lamar Jackson. It's worth noting the highly elusive QB didn't seem to break pocket as much as he might in live action, but the team periods were one-sided on both days. Flores will be able to create multiple different packages and pressure looks with his system. The d-line looks capable of getting into the backfield from time to time on pass plays or for run stuffs, and the linebackers' blitzes could be quite a calling card, given what Blake Cashman and Eric Wilson have accomplished so far in this scheme. Andrew Van Ginkel is one of one for this system, and Dallas Turner's growth as an edge rusher was on full display Thursday against two-time Pro Bowl left tackle Ronnie Stanley. Elijah Williams Is the real deal. Please let him make the roster. Honestly, we have a good DL. Why did we draft more depth? I understand, but we need help other places and the DL wasn't it. How about edge and linebacker or corner. We miss a lot when you look back at draft. Banks looked like he should have gotten draft in Round 2 but not in the first round. What do you think? We're deep on WR, which also makes me think Jordan Addison won't get a deal. What is your opinion? Demond Claiborne looks good. A year under his belt, he would be a monster. Williams isn't the only player on Minnesota's roster who is easy to root for based on a vivacious personality. He's often flashing a smile to and from the locker room but also means business between the lines. How cool was it for the Jersey City native to record a sack in Preseason 1 just minutes from his hometown? I've already touched on the merits of Banks and Orange in earlier responses, but Minnesota parted ways with Jonathan Allen and Javon Hargrave in the offseason. That's two starting roles to fill, and Minnesota likes the projection of what Banks and Orange will accomplish. Other teams thought highly of Banks, and I don't believe he would have carried into the second round. It also appears that second-round pick Jake Golday is off to a great start of his career, too. While the Vikings d-line depth is probably stronger than other positions, it's a grueling position, and having a rotation to keep guys as fresh as possible is important. The trio of Justin Jefferson, Addison and Jauan Jennings could be one of the best in the NFL in 2026. Beyond that trio, the Vikings don't have a ton of proven regular-season experience. Price and Felton have had some strong days in training camp and are also likely to help significantly on special teams. Claiborne's bounce to the outside for an explosive touchdown run to end the second-team offense's 2-minute drill is an encouraging element to add to a room led by Aaron Jones, Sr., and Jordan Mason, even though Claiborne has been bottlenecked in the preseason to 52 yards on 20 carries. Many of those have been short-yardage between the tackles, which likely will never be his bread and butter, but he got the call based on who was available to play at various junctures of games. He's learning at every turn. It's also worth pointing out the Vikings aren't scheming their runs to try to attack opponents' defenses. This Dillon Bell is very impressive with his size and speed. If they can coach him up to catch the ball, his run after catch could be off the charts. Bell is listed at 6-foot, 209 pounds and has shown his ability to pop on a couple of run plays (two at New York for 27 yards with a long of 17). He's also caught six passes for 51 yards so far. title: Why Did Banking Stocks GS, JPM, BAC Surge To 52-Week Highs Today? - Stocktwits
content: Shares of Goldman Sachs Group, Inc. (GS), JPMorgan Chase & Co. (JPM), and Bank of America Corp. (BAC) surged to annual highs after the banks posted stellar second-quarter earnings results that beat market expectations. GS stock led the climb among banking stocks, surging more than 9% after its record Q2 results triggered a buy-in. JPM stock rose 2.5% after its results surged past Wall Street expectations, while BAC stock also soared nearly 2% to a record high. GS stock climbed to a record high of $1,143.84 on Tuesday after the company reported record Q2 results that tore past analysts’ expectations. Goldman Sachs posted quarterly revenue of $20.98 billion, significantly higher than Wall Street's $16.4 billion estimate, according to Koyfin data. The investment bank also reported earnings of $15.91 per share, ahead of the $14.40 consensus estimate, while net income reached a record $6.32 billion for the quarter. The strong results were fueled by robust performance in investment banking, equities trading, and asset management, as companies continued to tap capital markets and pursue AI-related financing and strategic deals. "There's a lot of capital out there," CEO David Solomon said in an interview with CNBC on Tuesday. "I'm not concerned about the ability for the capital to be available for things that make sense." Shares of Rocket Lab (RKLB) rebounded after a six-session losing streak on Tuesday as CEO Peter Beck highlighted the company as one of the few proven commercial launch providers, calling SpaceX a “friendly rival” and noting that Rocket Lab emerged from a field of more than 100 failed challengers. RKLB stock jumped nearly 3% on Tuesday, with shares also up nearly 2% overnight. In a recent BBC interview, Beck said commercial launch remains exceptionally difficult despite billions of dollars in investment. “Despite billions of dollars and over 100 companies trying, there has actually only been two companies to pop out the other end,” with a regular and reliable launch service, he said, in a discussion that also touched on Rocket Lab’s rivalry with SpaceX. “Launch and a commercial company doing launch still remains extremely rare,” Beck added. Beck called SpaceX a “friendly rival” and said space companies often compete for one contract before working together on another: “You can be competing tooth and tail for a particular contract” and later team up to deliver it, he said. Rocket Lab can also benefit when rivals win as it supplies components such as reaction wheels, star trackers and solar panels.” “We can go head to head with a traditional space prime and then lose,” Beck said. “And then the next day, there’s a purchase order.” Beck called Rocket Lab an end-to-end space company spanning satellites, launch and services from orbit: “We build satellites, we launch them on our rockets and we provide services from space,” he said. Pointing to SpaceX’s Falcon 9 and Starlink model, Beck added: “They’re able to do all those things. And we’re able to do those too.” William Blair analyst Louie DiPalma recently named Rocket Lab and Blue Origin among the strongest challengers to SpaceX, though he said SpaceX still holds more than 90% of the launch market. Rocket Lab is advancing its competitive vertical integration strategy through its $8 billion acquisition of Iridium Communications, which would add a global network, spectrum, and recurring satellite service revenue. The company recently completed a full-duration burn of its Archimedes Vacuum engine, an important step toward the first flight of its reusable Neutron rocket. Rocket Lab said it was “critical preparation for Neutron’s first flight.” Beck has told Stocktwits earlier that Rocket Lab is “pushing very hard” to launch Neutron by the fourth quarter of 2026, while cautioning that the challenge is not merely reaching orbit but proving the rocket can return and be reused. “If we just had to go up, it’s super easy, we’d be in orbit by now,” he previously said. Rocket Lab also completed the U.S. Space Force’s Victus Haze mission, launching 16 hours and 42 minutes after receiving notice and completing spacecraft commissioning and proximity operations ahead of schedule. The company supplied the launch vehicle, spacecraft and orbital operations under one contract, offering a practical demonstration of the integrated model Beck outlined in the interview. Could be an inflection point if positive.” For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com. Comments posted here will also appear on symbol pages. General Fusion Group Ltd. (GFUZ) made history on Monday, becoming the first pure-play nuclear fusion energy company to trade on a major public stock exchange. In an exclusive interview with Stocktwits, CEO Greg Twinney argued that fusion is not just a cleaner alternative to fission but is a fundamentally larger market opportunity. GFUZ stock surged 21% on its debut, added over 25% on Tuesday, and was trading about 2.5% lower in the overnight session. The Vancouver-based company, backed by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, among others, went public through a SPAC merger with Spring Valley Acquisition Corp. III, which provided General Fusion with approximately $150 million in cash. Earlier, Twinney told the Wall Street Journal that the funding is sufficient to meet the scientific milestones required by its demonstration machine. The listing arrives at a pivotal moment. Surging electricity demand driven by the AI boom, the global spread of electrification, and the energy appetite of large-scale computing has renewed urgency around new sources of firm, clean power. Fusion has attracted growing investment and government attention as a potential long-term answer. According to the Financial Times, the number of private fusion companies has more than doubled over the past five years, intensifying competition at a time when the technology is still roughly a decade from commercialization. General Fusion is targeting its first commercial plant around 2035. Twinney's bull case for fusion starts with what it doesn't produce. Unlike fission, fusion does not generate long-lived radioactive waste, does not use fuels that could be weaponized, and carries no risk of a meltdown. "Fusion is just inherently safe. We're not needing to engineer safety into it in the same way that you need to with fission," he told Stocktwits. "When fusion fails, it kind of just fails safely and there's not really any fallout from that." That safety profile has a direct commercial implication: regulators around the world are moving to govern fusion "in a much lighter way" than conventional nuclear, Twinney said, which he believes creates the potential to site fusion plants closer to population centers and industrial demand. That's a significant advantage over fission, which requires remote, heavily secured facilities. "We get all the benefits that fission can provide without the downsides," he said. There's another significant advantage. Fusion reactors primarily use deuterium, which can be extracted from seawater and is "massively abundant." The other component, tritium, is rarer in nature but can be bred through the interaction of a neutron and lithium. Fission, by contrast, relies on uranium and other finite sources. "The overall market size because of the safety profile and the abundance of fuel in fusion is much bigger than fission," Twinney said. While advanced nuclear companies such as Oklo Inc. (OKLO) and NuScale Power Corp. (SMR) are often thought of as being closer to commercialization than fusion technology, Twinney said that the gap may not be as large as investors assume. While the road to commercialization for fusion technology has its challenges, including achieving reactor durability, tritium fuel breeding, economic viability, and the ability to efficiently extract and convert fusion energy into electricity, he argues small modular reactor (SMR) timelines also struggle with regulatory hurdles that can make timelines less predictable than they appear today. "I know that the timelines for SMRs, which can be very unpredictable due to regulations and those types of things, [are] probably not that different," he said. According to Twinney, the combination of abundant fuel supplies and a lighter regulatory framework could ultimately enable fusion to scale faster than conventional nuclear technologies once commercial viability has been demonstrated. However, Twinney does not view fusion and fission as mutually exclusive technologies. "They will be complementing each other," he said. "And I think that fusion kind of rounds out the nuclear circle if you think about it that way," he added. When asked about criticism from former Commonwealth Fusion Systems CTO Dan Brunner, who, in a recent interview with the Financial Times, said General Fusion's commercialization timeline was "very hard to believe," Twinney said the company’s timelines were based on real experimental results from its Lawson Machine 26. The machine is designed to demonstrate that plasma can be heated through mechanical compression rather than superconducting magnets or high-powered lasers, he said, adding that the company's early results validated the operating principles behind its MTF approach that are “not based on fiction or papers being written.” The timelines “are based on our real results from machines that we have built and operated and then eventually written papers on. But those are real results papers, not theoretical papers,” he said. Twinney also emphasized that General Fusion's approach could offer a cost advantage over many competing technologies. While many other fusion developers rely on expensive superconducting magnets, high-powered lasers, or advanced materials that have yet to be proven at commercial scale, General Fusion's Magnetized Target Fusion (MTF) system uses mechanical compression and a liquid-lithium wall that can protect reactor components from neutron damage, help with breeding tritium fuel, and absorbing fusion energy as heat that can be converted into electricity using conventional steam turbines. In an earlier interview with Stocktwits, Chief Strategy Officer Megan Wilson had also pointed to the economic advantages of MTF, which eliminate the need for expensive magnets, targets, lasers, or exotic, not-yet-invented materials. The technology also eliminates the need for frequent replacement of components damaged by neutron exposure, she had said. “Our plants are designed to be cost-competitive compared to coal, steam, and natural gas,” she had said then. “They are expected to deliver four times as much energy per unit of fuel as fission, without long-lived radioactive waste, positioning them as the superior nuclear technology for sustainable growth.” By avoiding costly magnets and lasers and using existing industrial technologies, Twinney said he believes General Fusion has a clearer path to building an economically viable power plant, as the company’s design has from the beginning aimed to avoid the major barriers to commercializing fusion. "What we are trying to do at General Fusion, and our power plant design from the beginning, has been we want to avoid the major barriers to commercializing fusion. Not just demonstrate a bunch of fusion, but actually avoid the barriers to commercializing it," he said. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around GFUZ stock is ‘bullish’ amid ‘high’ message volumes. title: LCK Enters Warring States Era, Halting Gen.G's Reign - 조선일보
content: Gen.G secures third straight regular season title but faces T1, Hanwha Lifee in playoffs amid intensified competition LCK (League of Legends Champions Korea) has entered a 'Spring and Autumn Warring States period' after five years. LCK concluded its 2026 regular season on the 23rd and will enter the postseason starting on the 26th. Due to participation in the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, the regular season was reduced by one round compared to last year. Gen.G secured the regular league title for the third consecutive year, including the 2024 spring and summer seasons. However, this season's notable trend was that Gen.G, which had established itself as the 'sole powerhouse' in the regular league over the past two years, showed signs of instability in performance from the early stages of the season, leading to a rare intense competition where the top spot was only confirmed in the final match. For the first time in five years since the 2021 summer season, there was no absolute powerhouse dominating the league. Both the 'Legend Group' consisting of the top five teams and the 'Rise Group' made up of the bottom five teams in rounds 3–4 engaged in fierce competition for rankings until the final stages. Gen.G suffered a 1–2 comeback defeat against DiPlus KIA in the final regular season match held on the 22nd. Gen.G took the first set, giving them an advantage in set differential and head-to-head record against second-place Hanwha Lifee Sports. However, they lost the next two sets, securing the top spot somewhat awkwardly. This was a far cry from Gen.G's dominant performance last year, where they suffered only one loss in the single-season format, and two years ago, when they had one loss per season during the split spring and summer seasons. While the team's morale was shaken by late reports of tax evasion allegations surrounding captain 'Ruler' Park Jae-hyuk at the beginning of the season, a more fundamental analysis points to the improved counterplay from opposing teams. Although the current roster has been cohesive for two years, making their teamwork even stronger, opposing teams have accumulated more data and experience to analyze Gen.G. Additionally, the ever-changing meta made it difficult for Gen.G to consistently maintain their previous strengths. The growth of rival teams cannot be overlooked. T1, the eternal rival, showed fluctuations in performance due to fatigue from participating in various international tournaments like MSI and EWC, yet still maintained top-tier competitiveness. Hanwha Lifee Sports, which has formed a three-way power structure with Gen.G and T1 since two years ago, also continued to deliver consistent performance, including an MSI championship, and competed with Gen.G for the top spot until the end. Although Gen.G did not dominate as they did in the past two years, the numerous trials and errors experienced amidst fierce league competition hold significance as they prepare for the playoffs and subsequent international tournaments. Particularly, if Gen.G aims to reach the Worlds (League of Legends World Championship) final and secure the title, which they have yet to achieve since their rebranding, addressing the weaknesses and variables exposed during this season's regular league has become a crucial task. Gen.G has directly advanced to the second round of the playoffs. The winner of the final match between Hanwha Life and T1 on the 23rd will also proceed directly to the second round, while the losing team and fourth-place DiPlus will begin the postseason in the first round of the playoffs. Prior to the playoffs, the 'Play-In' stage will feature KT Rolster, ranked fifth in the Legend Group, facing the top three teams from the Rise Group: Hanjin Brion, BNK Piorx, and Nongshim Red Force. Two teams that survive the Play-In, held from the 26th to the 28th, will join the playoffs.
